The chapter says the EASTERN part of Brazil is rich in various types of minerals — iron ore, manganese, nickel, copper, bauxite, tungsten and diamonds — and that mining has developed well in the highland region because of increasing demand in the country.

The interior and western parts are a different matter. The chapter names three limitations there: inaccessibility, lack of knowledge of the potential reserves of resources, and dense forests.

A mine can only work if the deposit is known, if it can be reached and if what is dug can be carried away. In the west of Brazil the land is covered by thick equatorial rainforest, transport links are poor and the reserves are not properly surveyed, so mining has not developed there.

**Similarities.** Both countries have long coastlines and fishing is an important activity in both. Brazil has a sea coast of around 7,400 km with excellent fishing grounds off the South Atlantic coast; India too has a long coastline and is one of the largest producers of fish. In both, fishing was traditionally carried on by small groups of individual fishermen, and in both it supports food supply and employment.

**Differences.** The reason for Brazil's best fishing ground is a meeting of ocean currents: the warm Brazil current and the cold Falkland current meet off the coast of south-east Brazil and make it a good fishing ground. Its main catch is swordfish, shrimp, lobsters and sardines, and although fishing was traditionally done with primitive techniques and equipment, large vessels are now being used.

India is one of the largest producers of fish both MARINE and INLAND, whereas in Brazil the fish resources of the Amazon River are not exploited much and inland fishing takes place only on a small scale — even though Brazil has a great many rivers. Fisheries in India help in augmenting food supply, generating employment, raising the nutritional level and earning foreign exchange, and fish forms an important part of the diet of many people living in the coastal areas of Kerala, West Bengal, Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Goa and Maharashtra.

Per capita land availability is the area of land divided by the number of people, so it depends on both.

Brazil is the fifth largest country in the world in area, occupying 5.6 per cent of the world's total land, but it holds only 2.78 per cent of the world's population, which gives it a density of about 23 persons per sq.km. India occupies only 2.41 per cent of the world's land while supporting 17.5 per cent of the world's population, giving a density of 382 persons per sq.km.

So a much larger area is shared among far fewer people in Brazil, and per capita land availability there is many times what it is in India. The chapter makes the same point about income: though India has a higher national income than Brazil, India's per capita income is lower, and it says India's per capita income seems even lower because India's size — that is, its population — is very large.

A mixed economy is one in which the government and private enterprise both take part in economic activity, instead of one or the other running everything.

The chapter says plainly that, like the Indian economy, the Brazilian economy is also a mixed economy.

The reason both took this course is that both are developing countries. They are progressing in technological advancement, education and industry, and their per capita incomes are still very low compared with developed countries like the USA. In such a country private enterprise alone cannot supply the capital and the services that development needs, and the state alone cannot supply the enterprise, so the two work side by side. Brazil is one of the world giants of mining, agriculture and manufacturing with a strong and rapidly growing service sector, while India is still dependent on agriculture though its service sector is also increasing.

The graph shows two things side by side for India and Brazil: how much each sector contributes to national income, and how much of the population works in it. Read off the bars, the shares are roughly:

| | India | Brazil |
|---|---|---|
| Contribution to national income — Primary | about 17% | about 5.5% |
| Contribution to national income — Secondary | about 26% | about 27.5% |
| Contribution to national income — Tertiary | about 57% | about 67% |
| Population engaged — Primary | about 49% | about 10% |
| Population engaged — Secondary | about 24% | about 19% |
| Population engaged — Tertiary | about 27% | about 71% |

The analysis:

In both countries the tertiary sector contributes the largest share of national income, which fits what the chapter says — Brazil has a strong and rapidly growing service sector, and the service sector is also increasing in India.

The striking feature is India's mismatch between the two halves of the graph. About half of India's population works in the primary sector but that sector produces only about a sixth of the national income, so output per worker in Indian agriculture is very low. This is what the chapter means when it says India is still dependent on agriculture, and it is part of why India's per capita income is lower than Brazil's even though its national income is higher.

Brazil shows no such mismatch. Only about a tenth of its people work in the primary sector, which produces about a twentieth of its income, while about seven in ten work in the tertiary sector, which produces about two-thirds of it. Its workforce and its income are distributed in much the same proportions.

Both are developing economies, but Brazil has moved much further out of primary activity than India has.
